```{r setup}
library(geopt)
```

Portuguese data usually identifies places in one of three ways: by official
code (the 4-digit DTMN for a municipality, the 6-digit DTMNFR for a
freguesia), by name, in whatever spelling the source uses, or by NUTS code.
This guide shows how to get each of them onto a map, and how to deal with the
usual problems: repeated names, lost leading zeros and spelling variants.

## Join by code when available

Codes are unambiguous, so use them whenever possible:

```{r by-code}
df <- data.frame(dtmn = c("1106", "1312"), value = c(20, 10))
m <- get_map("municipio", data = df, by = "dtmn")
```

Excel often turns `"0115"` into `115`. geopt restores the leading zeros when
it joins. To fix a column directly:

```{r pad}
pt_pad_code(c(115, 1106), "municipio")
```

## Join by name

Names are matched by `pt_match()`, which ignores accents, case and
punctuation, and reads the abbreviations `S.`, `Sta.` and `Sto.` as São,
Santa and Santo:

```{r by-name}
df <- data.frame(concelho = c("porto", "CÂMARA DE LOBOS", "S. João da Madeira"),
                 value = c(1, 2, 3))
pt_match(df$concelho)
```

### Repeated names

Some names are shared: two municipalities are called **Lagoa** (one in Faro
district, one on São Miguel), and 196 freguesia names are used by more than
one freguesia. A name that fits more than one unit returns `NA` with a
warning. geopt never guesses:

```{r ambiguous}
pt_match("Lagoa")
```

There are two ways to say which one is meant. Add the region in brackets after
the name, as INE's files often do, or pass a `context`, the unit it belongs
to:

```{r disambiguate}
pt_match(c("Lagoa (Faro)", "Lagoa (Açores)", "Lagoa (R.A.A.)"), quiet = TRUE)

pt_match("Lagoa", context = "Faro", quiet = TRUE)
```

At freguesia level, repeated names are common, so always give the
municipality as context. No municipality has two freguesias with the same
name, so this always settles it:

```{r freg-context}
df <- data.frame(freg = c("Pinheiro", "Pinheiro"),
                 mun  = c("Guimarães", "Castro Daire"))
pt_match(df$freg, level = "freguesia", context = df$mun, quiet = TRUE)
```

### Names from older data

In 2013, about half of all freguesias were merged into *uniões de
freguesias*, and in 2025 some of them were split again. Names from before
2013 match the freguesia that covers the same place today, so a file from an
older census joins without being converted first:

```{r historic}
pt_match(c("Sé", "Maximinos"), level = "freguesia",
         context = "Braga", quiet = TRUE)
```

Both are now part of `União das freguesias de Braga (Maximinos, Sé e
Cividade)`. The report marks these matches as `"historic"`, which shows
how much of a join relied on old names. A name that is still in use always
takes priority over an old one, so this never changes what a current name
matches. Pass `historic = FALSE` to accept only current names.

To get the code each freguesia had before 2013 instead, pass
`admin_vintage = "2011"` (the map the 2011 census used). Each old freguesia
then keeps its own code, rather than sharing the code of the união it joined:

```{r historic-to}
pt_match(c("Sé", "Maximinos"), level = "freguesia", context = "Braga",
         admin_vintage = "2011", quiet = TRUE)
```

To convert the *values* in a dataset between these versions of the map, see
`pt_recode()` and `vignette("vintages")`.

### Spelling variants and typos

If a source consistently spells a name its own way, pass `aliases`:

```{r aliases}
pt_match("VN Gaia", aliases = c("VN Gaia" = "Vila Nova de Gaia"), quiet = TRUE)
```

For typos, turn on fuzzy matching (this needs the stringdist package). It
only runs on names that didn't match exactly, only accepts a candidate that
is clearly the closest, and reports every match it makes:

```{r fuzzy, eval = requireNamespace("stringdist", quietly = TRUE)}
pt_match("Guimaraess", fuzzy = TRUE)
```

### Checking what matched

Every result from `pt_match()` and `pt_join()` carries a report. Check it
before trusting a join:

```{r report}
res <- pt_match(c("Porto", "Lagoa", "Atlantis"), quiet = TRUE)
pt_match_report(res)
```

The `method` column says how each input was matched, or why it wasn't:

| `method` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code` | the input was an official code |
| `exact` | the name matched, once accents, case and punctuation were ignored |
| `loose` | the name matched once small words like "da" or "dos" were ignored |
| `historic` | the name is from an older map, such as one from before 2013 |
| `alias` | the name matched through `aliases` |
| `fuzzy` | a close spelling matched (only with `fuzzy = TRUE`) |
| `ambiguous` | more than one unit has this name: add a context |
| `context_unrecognized` | the given context isn't a unit geopt knows |
| `unmatched` | no unit has this name |
| `empty` | the input was empty or `NA` |

## Three ways to join

**`get_map(data =, by =)`** joins straight onto the boundaries, for maps:

```{r get-map-join, eval = FALSE}
m <- get_map("municipio", data = df, by = c(municipio = "concelho"))
```

**`pt_join()`** adds to the data frame the codes and the regions each unit
belongs to, for work that doesn't need a map. It only adds columns that have a
single value for each unit at the level joined on. Some municipalities are split
between several ULS, for example, so a join by municipality gets
`uls_municipio` rather than `uls` (see `vignette("health-geographies")`):

```{r pt-join}
df <- data.frame(concelho = c("Porto", "Águeda"), value = c(1, 2))
out <- pt_join(df, by = c(municipio = "concelho"))
names(out)
```

Like `pt_match()`, `pt_join()` takes `admin_vintage` and `nuts_vintage`. INE
publishes freguesias on the 2013 map, so for its data `admin_vintage = "2013"`
(or `"auto"`) keeps the 2013 codes and adds that map's names, and
`nuts_vintage` picks the NUTS revision of the regions added:

```{r pt-join-vintage}
ine <- data.frame(dtmnfr = "030882", value = 3)  # a união split in 2025
pt_join(ine, by = "dtmnfr", admin_vintage = "2013")[, c("dtmnfr", "freguesia", "municipio")]
```

**`pt_lookup()`** returns the table of codes and regions itself, as a plain
data frame, ready for any other kind of join. Health columns are only added
when `health_vintage` says which version of the health map to use:

```{r codes-direct}
codes <- pt_lookup(health_vintage = "2024")
head(codes[, c("dtmnfr", "freguesia", "dtmn", "municipio", "nuts3_cod", "unit")])
```

## Cleaning names directly

The name cleaning that `pt_match()` uses is available as `pt_normalize()`, so
the same rules can be applied to any column before a manual join:

```{r normalize}
pt_normalize(c("S. Jorge", "SÃO JORGE", "Sao-Jorge"))
```
